why_this_disease_happens: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and progressive coronary stenosis arise from the retention and subendothelial oxidation of circulating apolipoprotein B-100-containing low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles within medium- and large-sized arterial walls. Chronic endothelial injury—exacerbated by systemic vascular inflammation, shear stress, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia—increases arterial wall permeability. Circulating LDL particles permeate into the tunica intima, where they tether to extracellular matrix proteoglycans and undergo oxidative modification by lipoxygenases and reactive oxygen species into ox-LDL. Subendothelial ox-LDL acts as an inflammatory danger-associated molecular pattern (DAMP), stimulating endothelial cells to upregulate intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1). Recruited monocytes differentiate into macrophages that express scavenger receptors (SR-A1, CD36) and ingest modified lipids without downregulatory feedback, becoming foam cells. Expanding necrotic lipid cores, chronic subclinical inflammation (quantified by elevated hs-CRP), and fibrous cap thinning by macrophage-derived matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) place plaques at high risk for acute fibrous cap rupture and occlusive intra-arterial thrombosis. Halting plaque progression and stabilizing vascular endothelium requires maximal clearance of circulating atherogenic lipoproteins via selective hepatic HMG-CoA reductase inhibition and profound upregulation of hepatic LDL receptors.
how_this_medicine_fights_it: Provides high-potency, concentration-dependent lipid-lowering and cardioprotective stabilization through stereospecific competitive inhibition of rate-limiting hepatic cholesterol synthesis, coupled with hydrophilic hepatoselectivity: (1) Hydrophilic Molecular Architecture & Hepatic OATP1B1 Uptake: Rosuvastatin ((3R,5S,6E)-7-[4-(4-fluorophenyl)-6-isopropyl-2-[methyl(methylsulfonyl)amino]pyrimidin-5-yl]-3,5-dihydroxyhept-6-enoic acid) is a synthetic, enantiopure, fluorinated pyrimidine-based statin. Unlike lipophilic statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin) that passively penetrate extrahepatic non-target tissues (such as skeletal muscle myocytes), rosuvastatin contains a polar methane-sulfonamide group, rendering it distinctly hydrophilic. Its cellular entry is driven selectively into hepatocytes via active carrier-mediated uptake through hepatic Organic Anion Transporting Polypeptide 1B1 and 1B3 (OATP1B1/OATP1B3) and sodium-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP), conferring high hepatoselectivity with reduced non-specific systemic skeletal myocyte exposure. (2) Nanomolar Reversible HMG-CoA Reductase Blockade: Once inside the hepatocyte, rosuvastatin binds with sub-nanomolar affinity (Ki ~0.1 nM; 4- to 8-fold higher binding affinity than atorvastatin) to the active catalytic pocket of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase. Its fluorophenyl group and polar sulfonamide moiety establish multiple electrostatic hydrogen bonds and van der Waals interactions with target enzyme residues (Arg590, Ser684), blocking the four-electron reduction of HMG-CoA into mevalonate. (3) SCAP/SREBP-2 Activation & Hepatic LDL Receptor Endocytosis: Intracellular depletion of microsomal free cholesterol triggers conformational activation of the SCAP/SREBP-2 complex in the endoplasmic reticulum, facilitating its trafficking to the Golgi apparatus for proteolytic cleavage. Active SREBP-2 translocates to the nucleus, binding sterol regulatory elements (SRE-1) to upregulate transcription and cell-surface recycling of high-affinity LDL receptors (LDLR). Upregulated LDLRs clear ApoB-100 and ApoE-containing atherogenic lipoproteins (LDL, VLDL, and IDL) from circulating blood via clathrin-mediated endocytosis, achieving 52% to 63% reductions in plasma LDL-C alongside significant triglyceride lowering and HDL-C elevation. (4) Prolonged Half-Life & Circadian Flexibility: Rosuvastatin has a terminal plasma elimination half-life of approximately 19 hours, providing continuous 24-hour HMG-CoA reductase suppression and allowing flexible once-daily dosing at any time of day. (5) Non-Lipid Pleiotropic Cardioprotection: Beyond lipid reduction, by halting mevalonate production rosuvastatin depletes isoprenoid intermediates (farnesyl pyrophosphate, geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate), attenuating Rho/Rac GTPase activation. This upregulates endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), improves flow-mediated coronary vasodilation, reduces vascular smooth muscle proliferation, and significantly lowers systemic vascular inflammatory biomarkers (hs-CRP reduction of 37% to 44%, as established in the landmark JUPITER trial).

Statin-Associated Muscle Symptoms (SAMS) & Rhabdomyolysis Surveillance: Like all statins, rosuvastatin carries a dose-dependent risk of muscle toxicity ranging from mild myalgias to myositis (CK > 10x ULN) and rare, potentially fatal rhabdomyolysis. Rhabdomyolysis manifests as generalized muscle pain, severe weakness, massive serum CK elevation (>40x ULN), and myoglobinuria causing acute renal failure. Instruct patients to report unexplained muscle soreness, tenderness, or dark brown urine immediately. DISCONTINUE ROSUVASTATIN IMMEDIATELY if markedly elevated CK levels occur or if myopathy is diagnosed or suspected.

Asian Pharmacogenomic Sensitivity Mandate (2-Fold AUC Surge): Extensive pharmacokinetic studies demonstrate that individuals of Asian descent (including South Asian, Indian, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Filipino populations) exhibit an approximate 2-FOLD ELEVATION IN MEDIAN ROSUVASTATIN AUC AND PEAK PLASMA CONCENTRATIONS compared to Caucasian controls, driven by higher prevalence of SLCO1B1 (OATP1B1) and ABCG2 (BCRP) genetic polymorphisms. IN ASIAN PATIENTS, INITIATE THERAPY AT 5 MG ONCE DAILY. THE MAXIMUM 40 MG DOSE IS GENERALLY CONTRAINDICATED OR AVOIDED IN THIS POPULATION; 20 MG ONCE DAILY SERVES AS THE CLINICAL CEILING FOR HIGH-INTENSITY MANAGEMENT.

Minimal CYP3A4 Metabolism Advantage (Reduced Drug Interactions): Unlike lipophilic statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin, lovastatin) that are heavily cleared by hepatic Cytochrome P450 3A4, rosuvastatin undergoes minimal (~10%) metabolism, mediated primarily by CYP2C9. IT DOES NOT INTERACT WITH POTENT CYP3A4 INHIBITORS (such as Clarithromycin, Itraconazole, Ketoconazole, or Grapefruit Juice). However, it remains a sensitive substrate for hepatic uptake transporter OATP1B1 and efflux transporter BCRP: co-administration with Cyclosporine (7-fold AUC surge), Fostamatinib, or specific antiviral regimens (Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir) causes marked systemic drug surges requiring dose restrictions.

Renal Impairment Titration & Dose Ceiling Protocol: Unlike atorvastatin (which is cleared >98% through biliary/fecal pathways and needs no renal dose adjustment), rosuvastatin undergoes roughly 10% to 28% renal elimination. In patients with severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30 mL/min/1.73m² not on hemodialysis), plasma concentrations increase 3-fold: INITIATE AT 5 MG ONCE DAILY; DO NOT EXCEED 10 MG ONCE DAILY. The 40 mg dose is strictly contraindicated in severe renal disease.

Transient Dipstick Proteinuria & Tubular Handling: In clinical trials, dipstick-positive proteinuria (predominantly tubular microalbuminuria, shifting from negative/trace to ++ or greater) was observed in patients receiving high-dose rosuvastatin (particularly 40mg). This effect is related to inhibition of receptor-mediated endocytosis of low-molecular-weight proteins in proximal renal tubules rather than glomerular injury, and is typically transient without progressive renal decline. Routine dose reduction is not required unless sustained unexplained renal deterioration occurs.

High-Intensity LDL-C Drop Profile (Comparison to Atorvastatin): Milligram-for-milligram, rosuvastatin produces the deepest percentage LDL-C reduction among all oral statins. Rosuvastatin 10mg achieves an average LDL-C drop of ~46% to 50%, while Rosuvastatin 20mg and 40mg produce reductions of 52% to 63%, making 20mg a reliable first-line single agent to reach the stringent 2026 ESC/ACC LDL-C targets (<55 mg/dL) for extreme ASCVD risk.

Antacid Chelation & Dissolution Reduction: Concurrent ingestion with antacid suspensions containing aluminum and magnesium hydroxide decreases rosuvastatin plasma concentrations by approximately 50%. Administer antacids at least 2 hours after rosuvastatin intake.

why_this_disease_happens: Severe hypertriglyceridemia (fasting serum triglycerides > 500 to 1000 mg/dL) arises from an overproduction or impaired peripheral catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TRLs)—predominantly chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL). When circulating triglycerides exceed the saturation threshold of microvascular lipoprotein lipase (LPL), large chylomicrons accumulate in high concentrations. As chylomicrons pass through the microvasculature of the pancreas, they are exposed to pancreatic lipase leaking from acinar cells. Lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides into large concentrations of toxic, unbound free fatty acids (FFAs) and lysolecithins. These excessive FFAs exceed the binding capacity of serum albumin, self-assembling into detergent-like micellar aggregates that disrupt pancreatic capillary endothelial membranes, triggering microvascular ischemia, platelet thrombosis, acinar cell necrosis, and acute necrotizing pancreatitis. In mixed atherogenic dyslipidemia, elevated small dense LDL (sdLDL) particles and low HDL-C accelerate coronary atherogenesis. Lowering circulating triglycerides to prevent pancreatitis and mitigate atherogenic risk requires accelerating intravascular lipolysis of VLDL and chylomicrons while suppressing hepatic VLDL synthesis.
how_this_medicine_fights_it: Provides targeted lipolysis of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and apolipoprotein transcriptional modulation through selective activation of the nuclear transcription factor PPAR-alpha: (1) Prodrug Hydrolysis & Nanocrystal Bioavailability: Fenofibrate is the lipophilic isopropyl ester prodrug of fenofibric acid. Following absorption, tissue and plasma esterases rapidly cleave the ester bond into active fenofibric acid. In modern nanocrystal formulations (145mg), nanoparticle milling enhances dissolution kinetics, allowing complete absorption independent of dietary fat intake, whereas older micronized formulations (160mg/200mg) require meal co-ingestion for adequate bioavailability. (2) Nuclear PPAR-alpha Agonism & RXR Heterodimerization: Fenofibric acid diffuses into hepatocyte nuclei and binds with high stereospecific affinity to the Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor-alpha (PPAR-alpha). Ligand binding induces a conformational shift that recruits coactivators and promotes heterodimerization with the Retinoid X Receptor (RXR). The active PPAR-alpha/RXR heterodimer binds specific Peroxisome Proliferator Response Elements (PPREs) within the promoter regions of target lipid-metabolism genes. (3) Lipoprotein Lipase (LPL) Activation & ApoC-III Repression: PPAR-alpha activation dramatically upregulates the transcription of Lipoprotein Lipase (LPL) while transcriptionally repressing Apolipoprotein C-III (ApoC-III), an endogenous LPL inhibitor. Uninhibited LPL anchored to vascular endothelial surfaces rapidly hydrolyzes core triglycerides in circulating chylomicrons and VLDL into free fatty acids and glycerol, accelerating triglyceride clearance from plasma by 30% to 55%. (4) Downregulation of Hepatic VLDL Assembly & Fatty Acid Beta-Oxidation: Fenofibrate upregulates genes encoding hepatic fatty acid transport proteins and mitochondrial beta-oxidation enzymes (acyl-CoA oxidase, carnitine palmitoyltransferase). This shunts free fatty acids into mitochondrial oxidation and away from diacylglycerol esterification, reducing hepatic VLDL-triglyceride synthesis and secretion. (5) Upregulation of ApoA-I, ApoA-II & Reverse Cholesterol Transport: PPAR-alpha stimulates hepatic gene expression of Apolipoprotein A-I and Apolipoprotein A-II, the structural apolipoproteins of High-Density Lipoprotein (HDL). This expands circulating HDL pools, elevates serum HDL-C by 10% to 25%, and enhances ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1)-mediated reverse cholesterol transport. (6) Microvascular Protection in Diabetic Retinopathy: As demonstrated in the landmark FIELD and ACCORD-Eye trials, fenofibrate reduces retinal capillary leakage, suppresses vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), downregulates retinal inflammation, and slows the progression of diabetic retinopathy independent of baseline lipid levels.

Pancreatitis Prevention Threshold Mandate: The primary guideline-directed indication for fenofibrate monotherapy is FASTING TRIGLYCERIDES ≥ 500 MG/DL (5.6 MMOL/L). In patients with triglycerides above this threshold, fibrate initiation takes clinical precedence over statin therapy to prevent acute hypertriglyceridemic necrotizing pancreatitis. Once triglycerides drop below 500 mg/dL, statin therapy can be initiated or optimized for ASCVD risk reduction.

Fenofibrate vs. Gemfibrozil (Statin Safety Distinction): Gemfibrozil strongly inhibits the hepatic glucuronidation enzyme UGT2B7 (which clears active statin hydroxy acids) and blocks hepatic uptake transporter OATP1B1, driving up statin plasma concentrations by 2- to 6-fold and multiplying rhabdomyolysis risk. IN CONTRAST, FENOFIBRATE DOES NOT INHIBIT UGT2B7 OR OATP1B1. When a fibrate is clinically required in combination with a statin, FENOFIBRATE IS THE ONLY RECOMMENDED FIBRATE. Gemfibrozil combined with any statin is strictly contraindicated.

Reversible Serum Creatinine Elevation Protocol: Fenofibrate therapy induces a dose-dependent, reversible rise in serum creatinine (typically 0.1 to 0.3 mg/dL, or ~15%) within the first 6 to 8 weeks of therapy. This elevation reflects down-regulation of intrarenal vasodilatory prostaglandins and competitive inhibition of renal tubular creatinine excretion, rather than acute tubular necrosis or loss of true GFR. Serum creatinine typically returns to baseline within 2 to 4 weeks after drug withdrawal. Monitor baseline renal function: if serum creatinine rises persistently > 30% above baseline, or if eGFR drops below 30 mL/min/1.73m², DISCONTINUE FENOFIBRATE.

Severe Renal Contraindication & Elimination Route: Fenofibric acid is eliminated predominantly (> 80%) by the kidneys as fenofibric acid glucuronide via glomerular filtration and tubular excretion. IN PATIENTS WITH SEVERE RENAL DYSFUNCTION (eGFR < 30 ML/MIN/1.73M²), FENOFIBRATE IS STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED due to significant systemic accumulation and severe muscle toxicity risk.

Warfarin Anticoagulant Potentiation (Severe Bleeding Hazard): Fenofibrate displaces warfarin from plasma albumin binding sites and mildly inhibits CYP2C9. When co-administered with oral vitamin K antagonists (Warfarin), IT STRONGLY POTENTIATES THE ANTICOAGULANT EFFECT AND ELEVATES THE INR. Reduce the initial warfarin dose by 30% to 50% upon initiating fenofibrate, and monitor prothrombin time/INR weekly until values stabilize.

Paradoxical LDL-C Elevation in Extreme Hypertriglyceridemia: In patients with baseline severe hypertriglyceridemia (chylomicronemia, triglycerides > 800 to 1000 mg/dL), rapid fenofibrate-mediated LPL activation accelerates the conversion of large VLDL into LDL particles faster than hepatic LDL receptors can clear them. Consequently, serum LDL-C may paradoxically rise by 15% to 35% as triglycerides drop. This represents a normal physiological shift from atherogenic remnant particles toward measurable LDL; if LDL-C rises above target once triglycerides are < 500 mg/dL, add low-dose statin or ezetimibe therapy.

Cholelithiasis (Gallstone Formation) Vigilance: Fibrate-mediated PPAR-alpha agonism downregulates cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP7A1, the rate-limiting enzyme in bile acid synthesis) while stimulating ABCG5/G8-mediated biliary cholesterol excretion. This increases the cholesterol saturation index of bile, predisposing patients to cholesterol gallstones. Discontinue therapy if symptomatic cholelithiasis or cholecystitis is confirmed by gallbladder ultrasound.

why_this_disease_happens: Atherogenic mixed dyslipidemia presents a multifaceted vascular threat characterized by the 'atherogenic lipid triad': elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), elevated triglyceride-rich remnant lipoproteins (VLDL, intermediate-density lipoproteins [IDL]), and low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C). The liver overproduces large, triglyceride-rich VLDL1 particles. Elevated intravascular triglycerides trigger cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) to exchange core triglycerides from VLDL into LDL and HDL particles in exchange for cholesteryl esters. Hepatic lipase subsequently hydrolyzes these triglyceride-enriched particles, generating small, dense LDL (sdLDL) particles and small, dysfunctional HDL that are cleared rapidly by the kidneys. Small dense LDL particles are highly atherogenic: they exhibit low affinity for the hepatic LDL receptor, prolonged circulatory residence time, enhanced susceptibility to oxidation into ox-LDL within the subendothelial space of coronary arteries, and avid binding to intimal proteoglycans. Standard statin monotherapy upregulates LDL receptors to clear buoyant LDL, but often leaves significant residual atherogenic triglyceride remnants and low HDL-C. Halting accelerated atherogenesis and reducing major adverse cardiac events (MACE) requires a dual-targeted approach: halting de novo cholesterol synthesis to upregulate LDL clearance while simultaneously activating nuclear transcription pathways to accelerate peripheral lipolysis of remnant triglycerides.

why_this_disease_happens: Atherothrombotic vascular occlusion and recurrent acute coronary syndrome (ACS) represent the combined consequence of subendothelial atherogenesis and intravascular platelet activation. In diseased arterial walls, high concentrations of circulating apolipoprotein B-containing low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles infiltrate the damaged coronary tunica intima, becoming oxidized into pro-inflammatory ox-LDL. Macrophages ingest ox-LDL to form foam cells, generating lipid-rich necrotic cores covered by a thin collagen fibrous cap. When shear stress or matrix metalloproteinases degrade this cap, the plaque fissures or ruptures. Rupture exposes subendothelial collagen and tissue factor directly to circulating blood. Circulating platelets instantly adhere via glycoprotein Ib/IX/V complexes to exposed von Willebrand factor, undergo shape change, and degranulate. Dense granules secrete adenosine diphosphate (ADP), which binds autocrine and paracrine P2Y1 and P2Y12 purinergic G-protein coupled receptors on adjacent platelets. Sustained P2Y12 activation inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering cyclic AMP (cAMP) and driving inside-out signaling that activates glycoprotein IIb/IIIa integrin receptors. Activated GPIIb/IIIa receptors bind circulating fibrinogen molecules, cross-linking hundreds of platelets into an occlusive, white atherothrombus that abruptly cuts off downstream coronary perfusion, precipitating acute myocardial infarction or fatal stent thrombosis. Halting post-PCI ischemic recurrence requires simultaneous dual intervention: stabilizing the underlying plaque by lowering circulating atherogenic cholesterol, while irreversibly blocking ADP-dependent platelet cross-linking.

Furthermore, atorvastatin depletes downstream isoprenoid intermediates (geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate), upregulating endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), reducing vascular inflammation (hs-CRP), and preventing further fibrous cap degradation. (3) Hepatic Cytochrome P450 Biotransformation (Clopidogrel): Clopidogrel is an inactive thienopyridine prodrug. Following intestinal absorption, roughly 85% is inactivated by human carboxylesterase-1 (CES1) into inactive carboxylic acid derivatives. Use with caution or consider temporarily holding statin therapy during short antimicrobial courses.

why_this_disease_happens: Atherothrombotic vascular catastrophe and post-stent occlusion arise from the interplay of fibrous plaque disruption and platelet-mediated microthrombus propagation. In advanced coronary atherosclerosis, continuous subendothelial entrapment of apolipoprotein B-100-containing low-density lipoproteins (LDL) triggers local lipid oxidation, recruitment of monocyte-derived macrophages, and necrotic lipid core expansion. Foam-cell secretion of inflammatory matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) thins the collagenous fibrous cap. When mechanical shear stress or cap erosion causes plaque rupture, subendothelial collagen, fibronectin, and tissue factor are exposed directly to arterial blood. Circulating blood platelets instantly tether and activate via dual complementary signaling cascades: (1) In the Cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) pathway, platelet membrane phospholipase A2 liberates arachidonic acid, which COX-1 converts into prostaglandin H2 and subsequently thromboxane A2 (TXA2)—a potent platelet activator and local vasoconstrictor; (2) In the purinergic pathway, dense granules secrete adenosine diphosphate (ADP), which binds autocrine G-protein coupled P2Y12 receptors, shutting down adenylyl cyclase and lowering cyclic AMP. Both pathways converge on the final common pathway of thrombosis: inside-out activation of platelet Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (GPIIb/IIIa, integrin alphaIIb-beta3) receptors. Activated GPIIb/IIIa binds multivalent plasma fibrinogen, cross-linking circulating platelets into a mechanical platelet plug that causes coronary artery occlusion or acute stent thrombosis. Solely blocking one pathway leaves the alternative activation loop vulnerable to ischemic breakthrough. Maximal secondary cardioprotection requires triple synergy: depleting circulating atherogenic sterols to stabilize the fibrous plaque while simultaneously shutting down both independent platelet activation pathways (COX-1 and P2Y12).
how_this_medicine_fights_it: Provides synchronized triple-pathway secondary cardioprotection by combining hepatic cholesterol biosynthesis arrest with complementary dual-pathway antiplatelet blockade (DAPT): (1) Enteric-Coated Polypill Engineering: Combines Atorvastatin Calcium (10 mg or 20 mg), Enteric-Coated Aspirin (75 mg), and Clopidogrel Bisulphate (75 mg) into a single capsule. The enteric polymer coating on the aspirin pellets prevents gastric dissolution, releasing aspirin only within the neutral pH of the duodenum to reduce direct gastric mucosal ulceration, while single-capsule co-formulation resolves post-MI non-adherence. (2) Endogenous Hepatic Sterol Biosynthesis Arrest (Atorvastatin): Atorvastatin enters hepatocytes and competitively inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, preventing mevalonate synthesis. Intracellular sterol depletion activates SREBP-2 cleavage and nuclear translocation, upregulating hepatic LDL receptors (LDLR) to clear circulating ApoB particles from plasma, lowering serum LDL-C by 36% to 45%. Atorvastatin also depletes downstream geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, upregulating endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), dampening vascular cell adhesion molecules (VCAM-1), reducing CRP, and inhibiting macrophage MMP production, preventing cap thinning. (3) Irreversible Platelet COX-1 Inactivation (Aspirin): Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) permanently inactivates the cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) enzyme in portal and systemic platelets by acetylating a specific serine residue (Ser-529) located deep within the hydrophobic catalytic channel. Because mature platelets lack nuclei and cannot synthesize new enzymes, COX-1 is irreversibly inhibited for the platelet's entire 7- to 10-day circulatory lifespan. This blocks the conversion of arachidonic acid to Thromboxane A2 (TXA2), suppressing TXA2-mediated platelet shape change, degranulation, and coronary vasoconstriction. (4) Irreversible P2Y12 Purinergic Blockade (Clopidogrel): Clopidogrel is an inactive thienopyridine prodrug bioactivated in the liver by CYP2C19, CYP1A2, and CYP3A4 into an active thiol metabolite. The reactive thiol forms a covalent disulfide bridge with free cysteine residues (Cys17, Cys270) on the platelet P2Y12 purinergic receptor, permanently preventing ADP binding. This preserves intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels, halts intracellular calcium mobilization, and prevents conformational activation of the GPIIb/IIIa receptor complex. (5) Synergistic DAPT Antithrombotic Power: By simultaneously blocking Thromboxane A2 production (via Aspirin) and ADP purinergic signaling (via Clopidogrel), this combination provides comprehensive Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT), preventing stent thrombosis, recurrent infarction, and cardiovascular mortality post-PCI.
